summary: Defines the MIME media type application/ogg for Ogg bitstream content carried over the internet. It is a proposed standard and was replaced by RFC 5334.

eli5.summary: When a file travels, it gets a label so the receiver knows what it is. This memo creates the label for Ogg files.

subtitle: Defining the MIME type for Ogg bitstream files.

tldr.problem: The Ogg Bitstream Format needed an official MIME media type so web servers and applications could identify and handle Ogg files correctly over the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3534 registers application/ogg as the MIME media type for Ogg bitstreams, allowing servers to label files and applications to recognize them.
tldr.outcome: The media type became standardized for use in web transactions and email. RFC 5334 later superseded this standard in 2008.

today: RFC 3534 is obsoleted by RFC 5334, which was published in 2008 and provides a revised media type registration for application/ogg and related types.

sections.title: What is the Ogg Bitstream Format
sections.content:
The Ogg Bitstream Format is a general-purpose framework for carrying multimedia content (such as audio or video) across the internet and storing it in files. It was developed as part of a project to create freely available and royalty-free codecs that anyone can implement in software or hardware.

The Ogg format provides a container that frames codec packets, allowing the receiver to find packet boundaries, recover from errors, and seek to specific points in a stream without needing to decode the entire content. This makes it suitable for both streaming (like TCP or RTP delivery) and storage (like files).
sections.eli5: Ogg is a box that holds audio or video data in a way that makes it easy to find where each piece starts and stops, even if something gets damaged.

sections.title: The application/ogg MIME Type
sections.content:
RFC 3534 registers application/ogg as the official MIME media type for Ogg bitstreams. The media type has no required parameters and no optional parameters.

Ogg files are binary data and must be encoded (such as with Base64) if sent by email or other text-only transports. The file extension is .ogg, and files begin with a magic number: the four bytes 0x4f 0x67 0x67 0x53, which spell OggS.
sections.eli5: The MIME type is a label that says "this is an Ogg file." Files starting with the letters OggS are recognized as Ogg format.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Ogg format itself is a rigid container format and carries no inherent security risks beyond those of any framing mechanism. However, applications that receive Ogg files must protect against malformed packets causing buffer overflows or similar attacks.

Since Ogg is a container, it can encapsulate any type of content, including executable code or malicious data. The receiving application is responsible for safely handling the content within. Ogg files are not signed or encrypted by the format itself, so external security mechanisms must be used if confidentiality or authenticity is required.
sections.eli5: An Ogg file is just a box; what matters is what is in it. Applications need to be careful not to crash when reading a broken Ogg file, and if you need to hide the content, you should encrypt it yourself.

sections.title: Uses and Interoperability
sections.content:
The Ogg format is widely implementable across computing platforms. A portable reference implementation is available under a BSD license, and the format is unpatented, allowing any third party to implement it without patent concerns.

Applications that use the application/ogg media type can encode or decode Ogg bitstreams. The format is typically used by audio codecs such as Vorbis, video codecs such as Theora, and subtitle formats, all of which benefit from Ogg's framing and error recovery features.
sections.eli5: Many programs on many computers can read and write Ogg files. Because there are no patents or licensing fees, anyone can build tools that use it.
